entry.title: Weeknotes for 9/16/2026
entry.content:
What A Week

In order to seem productive online, or at least prove that I am, I'm taking Simon's advice and posting a bit more about the things I'm working on. It doesn't seem like it'll matter much given how much LLM-driven traffic we've seen Google convert Web search into but here's hoping. Eventually, I'll be a bit more coherent but right now, I'm slowing down my work on Atmosphere projects and focusing on the desktop experience of Livtet; I'm focusing on shipping and making a GTM product so I can support myself.

Links

I'm waffling on this behavior of sharing the links to things I've read that I found interesting. I might populate a collection on semble so it's easier to follow if you're in the Atmosphere. I've included some notes and highlighting from the texts below.

Bundler belongs to the community

A quick history of how https://bundler.io/ came to be from Andre's narrative perspective.

AI Makes Better Software

Reading this actually motivated to take another look at what I'm doing with Livtet because it initially was supposed to just a desktop application but it blew up into this cross-platform monster of sorts thanks to a lot of tab completion with GLM and MiniMax. Namely, it helps:

"when used effectively and responsibly, delivers on the promises of agile development; ship a product, get feedback, iterate."

The Tower Keeps Rising

"The shared language of a software project is the common understanding shared among its developers. This language is rarely written down in one place but it lives in documentation and code. It can also just be something that comes up in code review or watercooler conversations or when one engineer has to explain a change to someone else,"

This, described by Armin, is also why it can take up to six months to fully onboard to a software project. Lore that simplifies the understanding of the code is shared by humans but has been simplified now by LLMs — to a degree. But:

"[i]n the days before agents some of that shared understanding was maintained by friction. If I wanted to change someone’s storage layer, I usually had to read their code and ask them questions. Changing that code might have required coordination with another team whose service depended on it. Some of this friction was useful as it forced communication. It also was a good touchpoint for both of us discover if we still understood how the system worked. I had plenty of experiences in my career where through conversations with my fellow engineer we collectively had to understand again why the system we had worked as it did before we did some changes to it"

— thus reducing the need for direct human-to-human collaboration.

Faulty Towers, vibe sickness, and the vibe bobsled

"If some of the best programmers in the world struggle to find bugs they even know must be there within a 100 line program, there is simply no hope for humans to review the volume of output from LLMs"

That's a very valid concern that Christine makes in their blog post. Software correctness is very hard and a skill that gets one the title of senior staff or principal engineers when done on demand.

Nobody pays for open source. We can force them to.

"The system isn't breaking. It's stable, at a level of human cost we've collectively decided to put up with. A maintainer burns out, somebody else picks it up, they burn out, and so on. Serial near-burnout isn't a bug in the equilibrium, it is the equilibrium"

That's a hard truth, but there's a bit of magic in:

"Developers write software the way singers sing, which is to say they'd do it if nobody was listening, and that isn't a problem to be fixed, it's the thing that makes the whole system work;"

— because people do this not for glory (sometimes) but for the hell of it. I'm hoping that this is the path registries end up taking.

Stalling installing

Jeremy writes about his plea (my words) to Apple to stop weakening the abilities to have Web applications become first-class citizens on their devices. I think we're going to need a EU-level-intervening on USB-C level event to get Apple to comply; it seems to be the only thing that works. They can always dance around the standards process by sheer force.

I wish folks in the Apple development community, after paying their $100 tithe were able to see how Apple is holding back the Web in so many ways.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 7/31/2026
entry.content:
It's weeknotes: link dump style!

I'm coming back to this style of posting what I've read, done and worked on instead of daily spamming on my microblogging accounts. Enjoy!

What I've Been Up to

I've been really heads down focusing on Livtet — I've made a decision to open source it so I have to rewrite a lot of the code and its setup to support it being open source while keeping some parts of the ecosystem I have for it closed. I'll write more about it next week.

Links

I've been reading a lot of what other people have been writing; here's a list:

  • atproto-fact-labeler (beta) is routing existing fact-checks onto Bluesky: This is awesome and I'm glad that something like this is being built in the open. I hate seeing bad posts that are nonfactual and provably false but being able to have something immediately highlight this is empowering.
  • Launching a Cloud Atlas: Erin Kissane's notorious for being a great wordsmith about the open social Web (or the social Internet as she posits as a better moniker). I wrote more about her piece and recommend it highly.
  • ATPROTO isn’t just for Bluesky weiners: Dan Abramov has been doing a lot of interviews recently working to promote and legitimize ATProto as The New Social protocol for the Internet. This is validating my own work with Olamaelcu!
  • The End of Reading is Here: Well. The title says it all but I had more thoughts on this topic. It's hard reading this while working on an app focused on literate folks but never say never! I felt worth expanding on.
  • A Social Filesystem: Now this was one that affirmed some stuff I knew. Dan worked at Bluesky and Facebook and has the ears of the tech industry's darlings. He supposes the idea of applying the personal computing concept of user-owned files to social media by creating a "social filesystem" where users maintain repositories containing all their data across different apps as structured records, rather than letting individual platforms store and control user content. This system, implemented through the AT Protocol, enables users to switch apps and hosting providers without losing their data, and allows multiple apps to work with the same data simultaneously, much like different programs can read the same file format. Safe to say that I'm super invested.
  • Where It's at://: This is a long blog post explaining how at:// URLs work using Rudy's post as an example, lol.
  • AI as a Tool for the Mental Load: I'm on the same page here. And frankly, as someone who's routinely overwhelmed, having a bit of a beep boop in the thinking flow has been helping.

Lots of posts about AT Protocol mainly because I'm building for and around it!

Books

I've been recommended to read Cutthroat and Verity — I'm still working my way through the first one and plan to start the second before the movie comes out. I'm also planning to finish my re-read of We Tried To Tell Y'all and start The Emancipated Spectator.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 4/4/2025
entry.content:
I'm back home from my two-week long trip out of Florida. Spending some time in New York City and San Francisco was good as I've been meaning to catch up with folks and touch grass of different areas. Doing it during Ramadan was even more enticing[1] as the reflection of time helped me remain more grounded (among other things) while in different areas.

Readings

I'm getting towards the end of Distributed Blackness by Andre Brock Jr. This book has me going back and forth on being able to recommend it and determining who exactly should read it. His approach to examining technology and culture (technoculture) through his self-described approach, critical technocultural discourse analysis (CTDA) has me agreeing in some places and furrowing my eyebrows in others. Either way, it's something that examines the holes in conventional understanding of modern computing, the labor it strip-mines for profit and the people who choose to exist despite it all. There's quite a few quotes I'd like to extract from my time reading the book that I'll probably upload to my Bookwyrm account at some point.

I'm slowly working my way through On Repentance and Repair, a phenomenal read that's already begun to change how I look at these ideas of care and reconciliation in my relationships; personal and beyond. Rabbi Ruttenberg's work in this space is informative; as I only know inklings around Judaism's tenants from cursory examination and reading[2]. I'd recommend this book to anyone who has and wants to strengthen the relationships they have in their lives - in all tenses of the term.

Writings & Learning

I haven't been blogging much outside of my week notes. Work has been all-consuming and my current state of life is changing, requiring me to focus more on it. I'm still working through my manuscript that I've gutted and rewritten about three times now for a fiction (once non-fiction!) book that I have to finish by the end of the year — for reasons. I expect it to be done by then but life is the dictator of my progress.

I've been taking Josh's class on React recently. He's a great instructor for a topic that I still find after ~5 years of working with this framework to be routinely exhausting. There's a reason why that I end up using Svelte each time — it just works with less of a learning curve and more out of the box that doesn't get in the way. It's a bit disappointing that what becomes popular is less about productivity and more about job security through obscurity and difficulty. But given the nature and formation of this industry, it's not terribly shocking. The course isn't cheap either; I'm fortunate that my job expensed the course and it's contributed to my productivity at work but having to do an additional hour each day to wrangle this framework due to constant questioning of its intent with me is more of a smell than I'd want to discuss here.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 3/14/2025
entry.content:
Happy Pi day! I'm more of a fan of tau but not here to slice things up. This week was met with a lot of reading; a return to Livtet and more planning for the rest of the year.

Writing

In lieu of the current focus of Canadian sovereignty under supposed threat by the current president of the United States, I wrote a short note about the nature of most colonial countries and the want for a broader lens in what's really going on. The sense of panic is unique in that it's afforded to a country that would never see itself ever being subject to some sort of foreign rule since it's done its time as a fellow imperial power. Something about leopards and faces comes to mind.

I wrote something short about the new direction I'm taking Livtet in. What I haven't mentioned but hinted at in that post is that I do want to make this into something folks can use for self-hosting and using to share their own libraries. I'm not sure if I'll host a service for the such but I do want to use this to add more options for folks in the social Web to share things that isn't just microblogging — we have so many things we can work with. This is my contribution!

Reading

I finished World Wide Waste on Monday and wrote my closing thoughts on the book on Bookwyrm. Some points were made in the book but it yoyo'd between blaming pollution and waste solely on consumers and then on companies themselves. I have a physical book and I have to say, it was hard reading the book. Without explicit markers for footnotes, I didn't know if I was reading the opinions of the author or if they were quotes — the extremely reduced use of typographical hints had me read each page about twice and open the associated links on my phone or browser to see what parts were quoted. You have to have time to read this kind of book and it's part of the reason why I avoided finishing it for some time. I want that time back. It is interesting to see the suggestions in this book be a bit of a soft retraction of things mentioned in an earlier book of McGovern from 1999 — what really provoked that?

I've been enjoying Lurking; a read on the evolution of folks' evolving relationship with the Internet. Some of it is before my time and exposure to the Internet but seeing the window at which they begin to overlap has given me some newfound understanding of how folks older than me (and more invested in the Web) choose to go about it. There's things in another book, Black Software, mentions but I was a bit sad to see the omission of some of the older Black social networks like AfroNet and the blogs. I think this is an attribute of the nascent nature of social networking history (it's still pretty novel of a field of research; ~30 years); but the notable ones like Black Planet were up there.

Other books that I'm reading slowly are World Eaters, The Spear Cuts Through the Water, Distributed Blackness and Haiti: State Against Nation when time permits during the week. I'm very eager to get deeper into Trouillot's works; I was inspired as I'm looking into the role that faith had in the Haitian Revolution[1].

entry.title: Weeknotes for 3/7/2025
entry.content:
I don't have any cable (or neo-cable) subscriptions anymore. I cancelled my Spotify ones as well. Being on their free plan is annoying enough that I'm tempted to delete my account. I do want to pay for the media I'm into but I can't justify the logics of paying for the slice of time in which I use it — I want to actually have the media. You know, like how folks would at least own DVDs in the 2000s[1]. Just because Warner Brothers and Sony decided to introduce a new profit model that works to keep them even more enriched doesn't mean I have to comply: they're not the law. Ironically, in cancelling more of these subscriptions, I had little reason to pull out my television — I only recently did to be ready to drop into a game of Mario Kart with a friend. But even that act feels too arresting — that of sitting in front of a TV. I just don't care for it anymore.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 2/28/2025
entry.content:
Closing out the month of reflection in the United States for Black Americans and their heritage, I found it necessary to return to my site for writing things out. I've drained so much energy and time into social networks, namely Instagram and BlueSky, with some level of reward but ones that diminish time and time again. This is routinely about what my expectations are with these platforms and I'm slowly learning that the longer one engages with these places (in a constant fashion; as opposed to taking breaks), the similar levels of disappointment (and developing resentment) that comes with it. From intentional misinterpretations of phrases to straight up fetishization of Black people, social networking has reminded me that it is in fact a reflection of "real life", the offline life; the world that choose to exist in and are able to curate to some capacity.

Sliding Back In

I've decided to pay more attention to the Microformats library such that I can unblock other folks from using it. Ideally, I'd like to get the types and library to a point of stability that I could have it become a flagship implementation. Taking it to embedded devices is something I'm very interested in doing. The approach that Microformats takes is one I've honed in because it enables one to use a Web browser - or a Web agent; meaning any device capable of talking with HTTP resources

  • to both style and declare information. It's also less lossy of a format than things like ActivityStreams and the flexible schema system of ATProto's Lexicon. There's a bit of comfort, also, in not having to reinvent the presentation and interaction layers; it's "just" the Web.

Latest Writings and Readings

I've finished a great book, How We Walk that a friend lent me[1], that invigorated my want to dive deeper into Fanonian ideas of decolonial psychology. It's something I've been more curious about as we've collectively slid into an acceptance of the destruction of the Uncanny Valley paradox and ignore the impact that such tools produce on a regular basis. It's perplexing and when things develop to be so, I turn to read.

I'm doing some cursoray research on the concept of ableism in the act of reading to confirm some ideas on it. It's not hidden that I'm an advocate for folks to engage literature. I do see that the most immediate form that one imagines when engaging with me would be that of a book. I'm not a purist of the medium that literature is held and consumed — I enjoy audiobooks, graphic novel renderings of books, video essays and of course, a physical printed book. It's not cheap to buy books — making me also a very big fan of libraries in all of the forms that they take place. I do want to make that more clear and look into making such alternatives more promiment when I bring material up. As with a lot of things under capitalism; the further it goes from a homogenous approach of use, the more challenging it can become to provide. That, however, isn't enough of an excuse to not try.

  1. This is my preferred vector of buying books! If I like a lot after reading it via the library or from a loan; I immediately get a copy. Books like Cultish, Tip of the Spear and Black Aboltionists have all become part of my annotated library because of this! ↩︎

entry.title: Weeknotes for 10/15/2024
entry.content:
Books

I finished Black Software; a read that begins with a journey of some folks who worked to bring in Black faces into the burgeoning tech industry. It closes with a focus on how the American government pioneered its War on Crime by using its historically racist approach to policing to mechanize technology against the American public — specifically against non-white people. It focuses on Black people but I can see these technologies being used against poor people of any creed — to be poor is to be effectively Black by the edicts of American policy.

I'm currently finishing up Their Eyes Were Watching God, a timely read that's a mix of an adventure book and a series of romance happening right here in Florida. I'm extremely tempted to go visit some of these places mentioned in the book like Eatonville and the Everglades. Hurtson has a way with words that transport you right into the moment.

New Job

Today's my first day working at Coforma — a government IT company focused on providing services for the American public. This continues my career focus on working in the public sector and public-sector-adjacent places. I'm eager to talk more about what kind of work I'll be doing in the coming months.

I have to thank everyone who've helped me get to this point. I have a bigger plan to demonstrate my appreciation that requires a bit of time to pass first but I'm really thankful and excited to see where things will go from here.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 8/26/2024
entry.content:
The month's coming to a close with four days left. I've all but finished my reading list for Black August, while managing to make some progress again with Livtet and picked up work again on Shock. I've added a new part to my site as well to document links I've been reading.

Reading

I'm realizing that, unless I have nothing else to do with my life (which is not likely), I won't finish the reading list I set out for Black August. I'm not disappointed, in fact, I'm very glad with the progress I've made of 4 out of 6 books for this month. Six was already a very high goal and I'm proud that I got this far.

We Do This 'Til We Free Us by Mariame Kaba

This book has been a roller-coaster. There's so many things I want to quote from this but I'll hold off until I finish Livtet so I can add more context. Kaba's interviews are a treasure because both the interviewers and her responses have expanded so much (and left me with even more questions on how I view prison abolition). It becomes more and more difficult to accept the mainstream idea that we need to punish people in a way that does nothing but expand the harms we claim to be against even more so.

You can view a lot of my thoughts (as well as others in the Fediverse) on the book so far over on Bookwyrm.

Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead

Listen, I am a fan of this man! I've read Apex Hides the Hurt by him and I loved the way he was able to talk such a difficult topic (integration of a Black and white neighborhood) with the overlay of branding. In Harlem Shuffle, he manages to do the same but with suspense. I am a bit disappointed with the ending but I understand why he did it that way. It relies a lot on a form of storytelling that's intrinsic to African American communities: that of the past to help design the future. I'm really glad that I got the ebook and audiobook combination for this; I imagine this kind of book being adaptable to some limited television series would go over pretty well.

You Exist Too Much by Zaina Arafat

This book threatened to make me cry and it almost succeeded, ha. The way Arafat closed the book was necessary and so healing — the need to understand where our definition of love comes from and how to evolve from it when it no longer serves us. Having to deal with family that refuses your identity in a country that refuses your identity is a double whammy that Arafat handles beautifully in this book; albeit in a drunken splendor.

None but the Righteous by Chantal James

This book is very different from ones I've read before. My knowledge of the South is limited and I've been working to expand that. James' approach to narrating this story; through the lens of a spirit is said to invoke the imagery of Toni Morrison's Beloved in a review. I haven't read anything from Morrison outside of The Source of Self Regard so this is both a learning exercise and a journey for me. Nonetheless, I am enjoying the story and eager to see Ham find what he's looking for (if he even knows what that is himself).

Writing

I wrote a longer piece about attempting to figure out how to engage people without holding resentment for the world; wrestling with the wrong ideas. I have yet to go through feedback for this post but it's something I'm hoping to routinely expand on. I've learned that a core component of being an activist - of any kind - is having a practice of self-reflection. I'm not the best at that.

Additionally, I've found myself wanting to write about links or essays I read in print or online and want to expand on what makes them interesting to me. I've written about adding bookmarks back to my site, in an IndieWeb fashion. entry.content:
Per the usual code, I was back to my books and working on Livtet. I managed to advance to the later stages of an interview process and I'm hoping for good news by the end of the month. There's also a potential of me picking up contract work. So far, August has been busy with reading and studying but there's growth and markers towards a bright September.

Reading

I'm still working on my abolitionist list for this month but I took some time to pick up some books I had hanging and hadn't finished yet.

Harlem Shuffle

This book is one I've been reading on and off; not because I didn't enjoy it but because the book was almost done. Big Mike's son has issue after issue crop up in his way of aiming to make a honest living. I got the audiobook to go with my borrowed digital copy and it felt like listening to a radio show; making the segmenting of the read even better. It takes place in a slightly alternate Harlem. It brings you through the development of the neighborhood and New York City in the 1960s. From riots to robberies, heists to heartache, this book is one I'll give to folks who are curious about New York City.

You Exist Too Much

A gripping tale of a Palestinian-American that's wrestling with love addiction[1], family drama and trauma and having to come to age in themselves. I wish I read this sooner and it's another book I didn't want to end. There were so many moments where I yelled at the book saying "GIRL NO" or "DUMP HIM"; I saw myself in some of these moments. The nature of being a Palestinian-American isn't hidden as the evolving genocidal nature of Israel is highlighted in the book. The nature of folks advocating of violence to these people unintentionally, with notions of a "two-state solution". Those events have reverberations in how the main character sees themselves and I'm glad that folks are writing humanizing material like this.

Prisons By Any Other Name

This book was getting harder and harder to read. So far, the book's discussed the level of violence waged by the state and private institutions against mothers who don't fit the "model" of an ideal parent. It also mentions the nature of the foster care system and its history as a religious-now-state sponsored child kidnapping program meant to force Native folks into "civil conformity". I'm currently on the chapter around the evolution of community policing creating "open air prisons". This chapter has a focus in New York City, which is my home city. The description of how the helicoptering policing of both cops and good-intention neighbors reminds me so much of my hometown. These kind of stories are grounded as the authors make the connection between community policing and the community murdering of Native people and slave capture committees. This book is definitely one that'll remain in my library of recommendations and I'm hoping that we won't need an expanded version anytime soon.

I didn't expect to finish the book this morning but I managed to. The last chapter on imagining alternatives reminds me so much of a quote attributed to Sadiya Hartman, that one of the greatest crimes of oppression is how deeply it has policed our ability to imagine[2].

The Trinity of Fundamentals

I'm reading this as part of the book club driven by Millennials are Killing Capitalism. I got this book last year when I went to 1804 Books's hub, the People's Forum, as well as a bunch of other books. I did not expect to be thrown so quickly into a world that was ripe with vigor and care.

For context, this book was smuggled out of the Zionist prisons set up in Palestine. It took 54 capsules of physical text to get this story, written over nine years. The way the book was written, I'm shocked that it hasn't covered things like the New York Times bestseller list. It's a gripping tale of the resistance development against occupation. It starts on a campus ground, showing the dynamism of the youth to learn and hold each other in political struggle while their homeland is being encroached by violence pushed on by the Reagan administration and the Israeli occupation. I'm doing my best not to run through this book because it's a page turner but it is hard.

Git Cute

I can't find much to say about this book; and in this case, this isn't necessarily a good thing. I don't want to speak ill of the author. I will say that I bought this book some time ago in support of them and in curiosity of what our experiences becoming a senior software engineer would look like. What I got from the book was something that, I think, you could find by examining software engineering culture on places like YouTube or Twitter. In fact, the book opens up with quite a bit about the nature of the marketing nature of software engineering (building a sort-of brand, for example). I can't say this is something I'd recommend.

Writing

I spent more time working on code this week — not much out of the blog. I did write about what I ended up working on. An extension system to Livtet using Lua; it was really rewarding!

Coding

As mentioned above, I got Lua working with Livtet. After writing that, I did a bit more tinkering to add in a stricter form for the system. The signatures for the API is a bit different but still has the same result. This was using another library, tealr, that also allows me to vendor a typed version of Lua via Teal. The difference is minimal but is more organized:

 local function items()
+ 	local user_profile = livtet.options:get("user_profile_url")
- 	local user_profile = livtet.options("user_profile_url")
 	local book_items = {}
 	for shelf, url in pairs(USER_URLS) do
 		local full_request_url = user_profile .. url
+		local feed_index = livtet.http:fetch_json(full_request_url)
-		local feed_index = livtet.fetch_json(full_request_url)
 		if feed_index ~= nil then
 			local first_url = feed_index["first"]
 			if first_url ~= nil then
 				book_items[shelf] = fetch_all_from_feed(first_url)
 			end
 		end
 	end

 	local books = {}

 	for shelf, book_list in pairs(book_items) do
 		for _, book_info in pairs(book_list) do
 			local book = expand_book(book_info)
 			table.insert(books, book)
 		end
 	end

 	return books
 end

I have yet to swap the use of things to use Teal as I'm still working on changing some things but I'm eager to report back on it.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 8/12/2024
entry.content:
I've been preoccupied with reading (as per usual) and focused still on the job hunt. I've also returned some time to playing video games! I also have some changing opinions on the current United States presidential race after reading some links and reflecting on my goals as well as that of the collective.

Reading

Prison By Any Other Name

This book was written by two abolitionists, one notably the EIC of Truthout. I'm finding this read to be more guiding and tangible for me than Prisons Make Us Safer. This is because it moves a bit from the introduction of aspects around the need for abolition and focuses on how existing companies, politicians and other institutions have a vested stake in maintaining these systems. It's also highlighting the lives of people who are forced to electronic monitoring (or EM) and the aggressive restricting that end up encouraging recidivism (the chances of re-entering jail or prison). It's hard not to see and get curious about the relationships of these companies mentioned to the industry I'm wading through.

Prisons Make Us Safer

I finished this book last week. It was written a year after Prisons By Any Other Name, both by the same author. I commend their ability to knock these stories out; they're not light and do a very difficult job of making plain institutional and commercial violence very plain. I want to write about this book because Law's done a great job of setting up common refrains for keeping prison infrastructure intact, like how it helps to keep children safe (it doesn't), how most people use abuse as an excuse to avoid jail (they don't), how prison is only an issue for men (it's really not), or how it's the most reliable way to keep us safe from rapists and murders (it's not). Each of these chapters bring you to talk about a point as to how these points go so popular and walks you through the lives of people impacted by these myths. It all returns to highlight one underlying aspect of society: that we are way more comfortable breaking up community than to work on healing or developing it.

You Exist Too Much

This book is one I'm returning to[1]. Arafat brings us into the mind of a young adult struggling with a particular addiction and identity crisis of both romantic identity and that of being a Palestinian-American. There's moments where I learn quite a bit about what it means to hold this kind of dual identity from someone of a different (and more recently publicized) background. There's also the growth (or steps towards — I'm not done yet!) of the main character aiming to grow a sense of self outside of what ails them — understanding what does it really mean to be loved. Excited to see how this book ends but she needs to tighten up!

No More Heroes

I opened this book on a whim because something about deconstructing the role of saviorship in mainstream media came to mind and this book had the word mentioned in it when I was searching my to-be-read list. The foreword by Roxanne Ortiz blew me away:

The author correctly begins this book with the Christian Crusades in 1096, and jumping across the Atlantic in 1492, as the foundation for the founding of a Republic (the United States) to “rescue” the Native. The very origin story of the United States forms the core of the savior project. In November 1620, English religious dissidents (“Pilgrims”) landed on the shore of what is now Cape Cod, Massachusetts. Forty-one of the “Pilgrims,” all men, wrote and signed the Mayflower Compact, named after the ship they arrived on. Invoking God’s name and declaring themselves loyal subjects of the king, the signatories announced that they had journeyed to North America “to plant the First Colony” and did therefore “Covenant and Combine ourselves together in a Civil Body Politic” to be governed by “just and equal Laws” enacted “for the general good of the Colony, unto which we promise all due submission and obedience.” A decade later, when additional English settlers founded the Massachusetts Bay Colony, they adopted an official seal designed in England prior to their journey. The central image depicts a near-naked native holding a harmless, flimsy-looking bow and arrow and inscribed with the plea, “Come over and help us.” Nearly three hundred years later, the official seal of the U.S. military veterans of the “Spanish-American War” (the invasion and occupation of Puerto Rico, Cuba, and the Philippines) showed a dark, naked woman kneeling before an armed U.S. soldier and a sailor, with a U.S. battleship in the background. One may trace this recurrent altruistic theme into the early twenty-first century, when the United States still invades countries under the guise of rescue.

I'm definitely going to keep reading this after Black August.

Eventually, this will be a bit more dynamic of a space; something that has links that I find worth writing about on my site and linking those notes here. It's a bit annoying to pull it out of Obsidian from here. Yet another thing to work on!

  • Inquest: Ferguson At Ten: This one was a hard read. Inquest did a great job of finding folks to help recap these moments. I think what's forgotten is the kind of administration we lived under, how much vitrol folks saw from the bipartianship committees and how almost nothing has changed to prevent these events from happening again.
  • Salon: Noah Lyles' collapse underscores our collective COVID denial: I'm upset for Lyles and the fact that we, as a society, have invested more resources in pretending that COVID hasn't happened at all. We have learned very little socially from the impacts of past pandemics and are more focused on the performance of a functional society as opposed to working to keep the health of it up. The fact that in four years, 1.2 million Americans have died from it shows this indifference quite loudly — and that's what been reported as deaths from COVID. We don't need to rely on the state to take care of us, however. It's a lot easier when our tax dollars can go to care and not committing genocide.
  • Comradery: Project Pages Update: Their first update in over a year(!), the cooperatively owned patronage platform is getting close to a beta release! I'm always eager to see folks explore this space.
  • Truthout: Last Week, 9 in 10 Americans Had No Opinion of Walz. That's About to Change: 1 out of 10 is still around 30 million people in the United States. That aside, Truthout provided a pretty balanced report on Walz and a set of stances as to why folks should be interested in throwing their support behind him. Despite my stances on artificial harm reduction; I think that having folks we can push is important. Labor seems to agree, although some unions are being more pointed about the hypocrisy held by the state.
  • Clear Thinking: Can astrologers use astrological charts to understand people's character and lives? Our new study put astrologers to the test: Astrology is something I have ... no real opinion on, to be honest. I try to understand it and have been combing over a book that Ra'il has suggested. I have friends who are practitioners and frankly, I have a bit more confidence in this, mainly because it requires to actually understand the person in question. However, this study does not help astrology as a concept (and flattens it - there's many different kinds of it) and shows some of the weakness of using empirical (secular) systems to define things that escape its measurements.
  • Ra'il: Black August 2024: Speaking of Ra'il, here's their plan on observing Black August! They have a different approach than I, which I appreicate because it shows the need to break from any sort of uniformity on how this goes down. The tenants are clear; the people diverse and so the practices have to reflect that. If you haven't yet, I recommend subscribing to their Patreon to support their work and their newsletter.
  • Prism Reports: Kamala Harris and the Erasure of Palestine: Something progressives and Democrats will repeat is the need for a "two-state solution", like the ones deployed in the United States and Indigineious nations that they've occupied. Harris is no different. Her background with Zionism is something I'm not too surprised about, in order to be a politican, you have to toe the line — no breaking from the talking points. One of those, for both Democrats and Republicans, is to see the complete eradication of Palestine from the map by way of the $800 billion+ US-sponsored genocide. The idea of "assimilation" is one that hits personally as the need for any non-Western European Anglo-presenting people to have everyone else adopt their identities, cultures, languages and lifestyles is something that still plagues us today. Now in the places where I live, I wouldn't be shocked if Harris does nothing to stop the increasing censure of free speech.
  • Prison Journalism Project: On Burger Day in Prison, I Went Back for Seconds: This hit hard. As part of Black August, I'm fasting, a practice meant to demonstrate solidarity with prisoners due to the inhumane approach to care that they receive. But to hear that a burger, something I can order on my phone if I'm lazy or make myself if I go outside to get ingredients, is made into something of a "reward". To learn that the act of bartering is illegal in Florida prisons, a practice that economists love to tout as the crux of the evolution of their field also frustates me but doesn't surprise me. Prisons are designed to dehumanize. The author, who's incarcerated in Everglades Correctional Instution out here in Florida, writes a lot about food.

entry.title: Weeknotes for 7/29/2024
entry.content:
Finally got around to reading some comics this week. I decided to restart my collection of the space opera Saga - it fails to disappoint!

Reading

I finished a book and am still working through a few others!

The Socialist Challenge Today

I've (regretfully) started this book, mainly due to its short size. The book aims to capture the difficulty of the formation of a socialist (or socialist-orientated) nation-state in the Western world. The calamity of the SYRIZA party in Greece was hard to read, due to the seemingly infinite roadblocks that they'd endure and the nature of being trapped within the Eurozone. Any action that they took would have to contest with global capitalism - a creation of the European nations that plagues them to this day. I ended up finishing it today and found the closing notes a bit sober (if not pointed):

The profound political dilemma this book has tried to confront is this: for a socialist-led government in the current conjuncture, giant steps toward transformative change would be impossible, but small steps risk being swallowed into the logic of the system. Even meeting the first condition for building on electoral success—i.e., immediately delivering material gains for the working class—entails being honest about the obstacles in the way. Taxing the 1 percent—or the top 5 or 10 percent—is a good idea for all kinds of obvious reasons. The potential gains from under taxed and untaxed corporate and financial income and assets, not to mention personal wealth taxes, inheritance taxes, luxury taxes, and so forth are enormous. But the capacity to do this without effective capital controls needs to be faced squarely. Moreover, the idea that taxing the "billionaire class" would be sufficient to pay for the impressive range of policies proposed by socialists today is clearly fanciful—and tends to underestimate the need for weaning the working class itself away from the anti-tax propaganda of the neo-liberal era.

It's meant to be a honest perspective but I do think there's a bit of an immediate concession on what could work and a hyper-focus on federal level reforms that, if coupled with state changes, like the one designed by Bernie in Vermont, could make this transition a lot easier. However, it doesn't seem like the authors have much faith (or excluded consideration) of state-level pressure that could be applied to push for federal change in a meaningful way. It's as if by shooting for the highest target, one is destined to fail. They do follow up with something that's not really unchallengeable without engaging in some form of nation-state violence:

An overriding limit in all of the steps toward taking control over economic life, even in the case of relatively modest expansions of social provision, is the power of capital to exit and invest abroad (along with the refusal of capital to keep coming in).

We see the above most nominally in places like Cuba, where the United States and its allies use the weight of nation-state commerce levers like embargoes and sanctions to restrict the ability of a country to build independence of its own means. This practice is a readily available aspect of Western capital via the levers of nation-states and it's an old practice. In another book, Haiti: State Against Nation, Trouillot highlights how European countries used this as a way to weaken Haiti's fledging economy out the gate:

At the first testing ground of neocolonialism, Haiti experienced the somber implications of that policy for the third world very early. As a neocolony of two industrializing countries, it collected from neither the now-expected (even if meager and unsatisfactory) returns of the post-colonial order. Foreign aid was not fashionable—not even in the name of strategic interests; nor were development programs. The United Nations did not exist; nor did the World Bank, the IMF, the Organization of American States, or the British Commonwealth. Haiti's trajectory was against the current; its very existence defied the geopolitical odds. It was an agricultural exporter, yet imported primarily agricultural products—indeed a peasant country where food topped the list of imports. It was a country born of a revolutionary war, yet one subordinated to the military power of Europe and the United States. ... At a time when European nations were extending their sway in African and when U.S forces were occupying the Philippines, Cuba and Puerto Rico, Haiti stood alone with Liberia and Ethiopia, black states in a modern international order where political independence was associated—as if in nature—with whiteness. It was a country without national allies, an international anachronism.

I will say, for a book that wants a socialist world, The Socialist Challenge focused a lot on the West (understandably) but failed to connect aspects of national and foreign policy that reinforces the control and mobility of capital that we see today[1].

How Europe Underdeveloped Africa

Rodney makes some points that remind me a lot of interactions I've seen today. Namely, emphasis made by me:

To ease their guilty consciences, Europeans try to throw the major responsibility for the slave trade on to the Africans. One European author of a book on the slave trade (appropriately entitled Sins of Our Father) explained how many other white people urged him to state that the trade was the responsibility of African chiefs, and that Europeans merely turned up to buy the captives — as though without European demand there would have been captives sitting on the beach by the millions.

I'm looking for a copy of that book to read because I'm curious about how these narratives were crafted. It was published in the 1970s in England so I'm expecting a smidgen of white victimhood being made into the central point of the book. It's safe to say that this book, and I'm only about a quarter in, is filling in the gaps I have in my understanding of the relationship that Europe had with Africa. Another point that stood out to me was Rodney's expansion on how "Europe became the center of a world-wide system and that it was European capitalism which set slavery and the Atlantic slave trade it motion". He writes:

Furthermore, when one European nation challenged another to obtain captives from an African ruler, Europe benfitted from whichever of the two nations won the conflict. Any European trader could arrive on the coast of West Africa and exploit the political differences which he found there. For example, in the small territory that the Portuguese later claimed as Guinea-Biassau, there were more than a dozen ethnic groups. It was so easy to see one off against another that the Europeans called it a "slave trader's paradise".

This invoked the imagery of the current "competition" that the United States and Canada had in picking which eager member of AFRICOM's watchful eye would be selected to send their troops to Haiti in order to "control the gang violence" that's gone to the national stage. In this case, Kenya, at the whim of William Rufo, is working with the PNH (Haiti's national police), decided to pick up that mantle last year. Embarrassing. Perhaps more embarrassing as wearing white wigs in an African state house. Decolonization is a lifestyle and journey.

Writing

I wrote two posts last week. One was about my growing frustration in finding a job. I've gotten some great chances to talk to folks on how to improve my chances and folks have been trying to connect me with roles. However, it's becoming more clear that positioning seems to be less of a reliable option and that a direct referral might be the only option. I recently had a chance at a contract role that effectively disappeared due to a change in requirements, something that really messed up my planning as they spoke as if I was to be starting within a week. I've come to trust nothing until my direct deposit information is taken and even then, not until I get my first check. It wasn't like this for me but it's increasingly clear that dehumanizing is core to business operations.

The other post was about the end of my discussion of electoral politics online. I gave reasons that reinforce my want to distance myself from the conversation. Outside of being directly blamed online for the preemptive election of a Republican candidate[2], I'm choosing to actively disengage with people who try to "educate" me on things. I routinely talk about my perspective on American, African and politics of the global South, being a party member of the All African People's Revolutionary Party and a labor organizer; it's necessary to understand as much as possible of the global context in which the world operates for one's activism to be meaningful beyond a little kickback.

Coding

I got the basis of search working and I replaced the command-line approach for getting book information from Calibre with a means of fetching information from its content server. I've made the logic for talking to the content server into a separate library, if for some reason, it can be useful to someone else and to begin isolating the remote places book information can be pulled from. I'm starting to focus on more what it looks like to view a particular book. The initial screenshot I shared in an earlier post no longer represents that and I'm hoping to have something neat by the end of this week.

Seeing

entry.title: Weeknotes for 7/22/2024
entry.content:
Last week was pretty noisy; both in the world and locally. I hope you're able to find some time to yourself and some ability to be in the community that'll keep you safe and grounded. I have a few calls this week for work and a potential lead; still early but things are looking up. That said, I'm open to a new role and eager to chat. I was planning on releasing this yesterday but I got wrapped up with stuff.

Reading

The Victorian Internet

I'm biased in favor of expanding "world history" to include the lives for those who are rarely recorded and deemed as more to be property of the wealthy. That said, I finished reading my copy of this book a few days ago. The book ended as it began, a mix of praise of the ingenuity of entrepreneurship and the undying zeal for human connection. At least that's how Standage reported it in repeating the recorded accounts of the time. I still can't help but notice a similarity in how technology of that time mirrors that of today. For example, Standage makes the claim that "the telegraph community was a meritocracy - it didn't matter who you were as long as you could send and receive messages quickly - which was one of the reasons that women and children were readily admitted to the profession" but on the following page highlights that once through the door when "a young operator had gained a foothold in a city office, he or she could expect to be subjected to a humiliating induction ritual, known as salting, [where] ... the operator would be sent bogus messages addressed to "L. E. Phant" or "Lynn C. Doyle" .. [that] the unwary beginner would be asked to operate a wire with a particularly fast sender at the other end, who would start sending at a reasonable rate but then gradually pick up the pace". I think the word meritocracy has rarely actually been deployed in a case where the definition mirrors reality and this example shows that. Following that, Thomas Edison, the golden child of the electric era, is praised for his ability to move quickly and grow. I think that, in reading this, I was expecting something that was going to speak more to the lives of people who were using and impacted by the (seemingly short) era of the telegraph. Instead, I got mainly the wealthier class of folks and the floundering of such a system.

That aside, the mobilization of effort, the amount of capital required, the international efforts to have countries agree on how to send, protect and handle messages and the way that telegraphy warped (and evolved) the public self hides something very lightly mentioned. Despite the sense of an erosion of borders and the melding of the "Old World with the New World", telegraphy technology effectively reinforced the need for building a nation-state in these times. Who else had the fulcrums of power (at that time) that could convince people to lay down cabling from England to New York? One could point to the early companies that did it but these required the blessing of the institutions that validated their corporate charters. It was critical in the American Civil War, as mentioned when "a total of 15,000 miles of telegraph wire" was laid down (which would also require constant protection and repair, most likely done in combination with technicians and the most expendable soldiers) to keep deployment and resources at high tally. I have more to say about this book and what I feel about it but that's for another post - I have to read a bit more about Standage himself. His narrative self both obscures some of these points and elevates I'm trying to flesh out and the book I'm hoping to use as a counterbalance will be Liberalism At Large.

Manufacturing Consent: The Political Economy of the Mass Media

I'm nearing the end of the book by Chomsky and Herman and I'm finding things in it that I can see had a huge indirect influence on how people are perceiving online journalism to exist today[1]. I'm finding it harder to not see how things like social media might have played heavily into the hands of corporate America to both weaken the trust in public journalism and reduce the resources spent on it as a whole.

Coding Books

I started Programming Interviews Exposed on a whim because nothing can hurt my chances right now in this job market. I don't have a lot of books about software in print because I find it a lot more useful to keep it open on one screen and work through examples on another. But this book had me pull up Zeal a lot more for remembering C++ primitives. I don't normally work with the language but the lack of the harnesses normally found in languages like JavaScript or even Rust felt actually a bit enjoyable[2]. Implementing the linked list was straight forward once I refreshed myself on initialization logic. I got way too used to Rust and JavaScript's approach.

Another book on code (though a bit more indirect and more on the theory) that I've started has been Practical Cryptography. The book is about twenty years old, which gives room for a fair amount of skepticism on the applicability of what's inside. That hasn't been the case for me so far. The book makes very good points about the nature of software engineering as being more subservient to satisfying the production needs of business and less on the security needs. There's an example of an office where locks are installed on each door and the immediate way how such a setup enables simpler hacking due to the physical weakness of the ceiling being artificial and the increased barrier for physical auditing by night-time security. The lesson from that, from what I gathered, was on making security less difficult to obscure and keep track of who has access to what and when they did so. There's things here that I can see being applied to the realm of organizing, as I do believe that there's a strong notion of weak surveillance by the State when they've been the main drivers of the growth of the systems that you use to view this text right now. It's something that's growing my interest in the concept and providing concepts like the aforementioned that I can bring back to my everyday work.

Coding

So it looks like I'm not alone on my venture to build The One True CMS. Jeff Eaton mentioned their work which reminds me a lot of what I want Shock to develop into. I've given up on making that happen in this year and instead focusing on just getting parts working such that I can get a Voltron-esque situation going. I've written about the current side-project to this, the plug-in/scripting/addons system I'm still fleshing out, while also reworking how I want the presentation of things to look. I haven't touched things like searching just yet but it's on the roadmap for next week as a bit of a stop-gap to the issue with the slow approach to loading content from Calibre at the moment.

entry.content:
People really showed out for my birthday. I appreciate y'all a lot. I now have enough to get me going until the end of August. I'm feeling more confident that I'll find a role by then. If you know of any software engineering opportunities (full-time or contract), hit me up. I got two new comic volumes!

Reading

I got Bitter Root v3 and Black Science v5. I haven't started either yet as I was focused on my current reading stack. Ideally, I'll do that this week.

The Victorian Internet was continued last week. Last week, I mentioned the role that Asiatic resources played into the development of the underwater cable. By now, I've gotten to the point where it was successfully built. It came very expensively. A person who resembles a white South African man that managed to tank the value of a social network managed to do nearly the same to the early crafting of the first Trans-Atlantic cable. The initial release was so bad and so frayed that "the official opening of the cable to public traffic was delayed again and again, and commercial messages started to pile up at both ends, while the true state of affairs was kept under wraps. The reliability of the cable steadily deteriorated, and it eventually stopped working altogether on September 1, less than a month after its completion" in 1858. I wish I had the level of disregard for society that Edward Whitehouse had - dude went to court and "as he attempted to defend himself and his flawed theories, Whitehouse blamed everyone around him. Portraying himself as a man of science struggling against the forces of ignorance and incompetence, he blamed the manufacturers of the cable, the crew of the ship that laid it and most of all, Cyrus Field and the other officials of the Atlantic Telegraph Company, who he claimed had refused to let him carry out all the tests he recommended. Built different, I say 🤣!

I've mentioned this in passing but I'm reading Manufacturing Consent. It's been taking me some time to read this, I do find it harder to parse books like this - a semi-narrative retelling and journalistic expansion of events. While reading this, I definitely made the connection this author is also the same computer linguistics guy. Talk about using your time productively, I guess? I'm a bit over halfway through the digital copy I'm reading. To be honest, I'm glad I read this digitally because searching for the references mentioned has prevented me from getting too distracted. It's also no surprise to me that the Heritage Foundation, the same one behind the policy book, Mandate for Leadership: A Conservative Promise are also the same ones who pushed for Congress to "buy the top academic reputations in the country to add credibility to corporate studies and give business a stronger voice on the campuses", quoted from the book. Chomsky notes this as formulaic of right-wing groups since the 1970s, potentially a response to the rise of revolutionary academics and rising student protests during the time. He writes, "the corporate funding and clear ideological purpose in the overall effort had no discernible effect on the credibility of the intellectuals so mobilized; on the contrary, the funding and pushing of their ideas catapulted them into the press". We see this with large media outlets like the New York Times[1]. I'm eager to finish this book but I'm taking my time.

I don't think I'll ever stop talking about The Source of Self Regard. Morrison is a true American writer. That'll ruffle the imagination of those who fixate on Twain and the like but I make this point because she writes about America in a way that few can touch and still manages to be clear and direct. She writes, "there is a clear flight from Blackness in a great deal of Afro-American literature", which is clear from the many media portrayals of Black people and the narrative of representation in spaces where it devolves slowly into how much capital (social, fiscal or otherwise) one has managed to accrue. It's rarely been about uplifting tangible community and is conventionally about transforming people into subscribers or assets. Spill is a great example of this. They have the explicit goal of selling people's content to advertisers who can optimize on knowing it's a platform of Black folks. Companies can visit this platform, as demanded by venture capitalists, to optimize their traffic, at the behest of two Black folks running the helm. I don't fault anyone for making money in a capitalist society but we can't be doing it at the cost of the privacy of our own people. Let Zuckerberg do that. Morrison doesn't make any explicit demands - at least not to the reader. The book begins with essays she's given to many organizations and graduating classes. I can't recommend it enough and I'm only halfway through the book.

Addendum

I also managed to get my copies of Cultish returned to me. I'll be looking forward to extracting my notes from my machine to add to the book[2]. There's books I'd like to start like The Utopia of Rules, The Crisis of Democratic Capitalism, Antiblackness and maybe The Rational Optimist. I have at least a dozen other books to start before I can actually open any of those but we don't follow rules here.

The goal of livtet[3] is to make something I can use to actually host next to this website, link things I've read and serve as a personal archive for my notes. Chris Ferdinandi's newsletter about ADHD is something that makes me think about needing this a lot, namely the need to dump everything[4]. This is one way for me to do that. It's going to be written in Rust using Tauri as I've been using that for a lot for things like Shock and other toy applications[5]. Feel free to drop any issues at https://todo.sr.ht/~jacky/livtet or send an e-mail to ~jacky/livtet@todo.sr.ht, no account required.

Felt semi-optimistic last week. Definitely went on a bit of a rant on Mastodon that made me wonder about how what I post online gets surfaced into search results and if that could be impacting my ability to find work. I guess I'll never really know - feedback is strictly limited to "I'm sorry". I'm still working on making a page to track this job hunt progress - the code is simple but it's more emotionally taxing than I expected.

Coding

I've been stuck on an issue with both getting Veilid running on my server and having my client application connect to a hub. I'm hoping to have something demonstrable by the end of the week because I'd love to contribute to the fledging world of applications experimenting with things like Veilid.

I've started working on an attempt to run Librecast on a mobile device using NativeScript. The code's still early as I'm focused on getting the native library to be callable from JavaScript. I initially wanted to use Neon but the docs are extremely sparse on initial setup. That led me to consider using napi-rs, something I'll begin experimenting with this week. It'll be interesting to see this work especially on a mobile device - my understanding is that most might not support IPv6 without being connected to WiFi. Again, I think I'm wrong here, hence why I'm even trying this.

Reading

I finished The One Device. It was definitely a trip and gives me a sobering perspective on the tech industry's allegiance to both Apple, Western hegemonic pushing towards hardware manufacturing and the things that prevent societies from grappling the inherently xenophobic underbelly that technology relies on in order to survive. You wouldn't know half of what's mentioned by reading the cover or the back - that's for sure. At the same time, Apple's more of the face of this moment and less of the engine. The majority of machines that require semi-conductors end up coming out of China, Taiwan or other regions forced to operate in "highly-skilled, low-wage" industrial-esque society.

I'm reading How Europe Underdeveloped Africa, a challenging read mainly because Rodney's focus on looking at how European development during the 1300s to the 1500s was influencing the world (Asiatic and Indian trade were impacted) forced a lot of reconsideration of the perspective of how development is taught in the United States. It also had me stop to understand that while trade is a required component of communal interactivity, if said trade is designed to create imbalance and forced scarcity, it can become a tool of socioeconomic policy making (if not all out economic war).

I've continued my reading of The Victorian Internet. Reading this as I'm reading the aforementioned book, I do have to imagine how European authors only manage to relegate the rest of the world as just places of exploit (if not places of material extraction). The passive note of how an Asiatic plant was crucial to the construction of the first Atlantic submerged electric cable that was necessary for cross-Atlantic communication felt similar to both what Rodney mentions in the denigration of external societies as a sort of battery for innovation (my words).
